panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A is a Masson's trichrome stained kidney histology section from a hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis patient showing fibrinoid necrosis of a pre-glomerular arteriole, a classic histologic manifestation of the disease matching the provided vocabulary finding. B: Panel B is a kidney histology section from a hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis patient showing global endocapillary proliferation and interstitial inflammatory infiltrate, but no findings match the provided vocabulary. C: Panel C is a kidney histology section from a hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis patient showing interstitial nephritis with mononuclear infiltrate and tubular damage, but no findings match the provided vocabulary. D: Panel D is a kidney immunofluorescence section from a hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis patient showing abundant C1q deposits in renal structures, but no findings match the provided vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Corthier et al. Biopsy-proven kidney involvement in hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis.. BMC nephrology 2022. doi:10.1186/s12882-022-02689-8. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Representative kidney pathological lesions observed in patients with Hypocomplementemic Urticarial Vasculitis from the present cohort. A Vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis involving a pre-glomerular arteriole. Masson’s trichrome, × 200. B Global endocapillary proliferation with an interstitium containing a slight peri-venular inflammatory infiltrate. Masson’s trichrome, × 200. C Interstitial nephritis with mononuclear cells, oedema, and suffering tubules. Masson’s trichrome, × 200. D Abundant deposits of C1q within arteriole wall, capsule, and tubular basement membrane. Immunofluorescence, × 200

panels.rationale: Clinical photograph from a case report of hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis showing urticarial-like exanthema with wheals on the face and discreet angioedema of the lips as described in the caption and accompanying text.
panels.attribution_text: Ion et al. Kidney Involvement in Hypocomplementemic Urticarial Vasculitis Syndrome-A Case-Based Review.. Journal of clinical medicine 2020. doi:10.3390/jcm9072131. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
in_text_mentions: Physical examination revealed pale skin, with urticarial–like flare involving the face and neck (Figure 3). The wheals were nonpruritic, mildly erythematous and palpable, and were associated with a discreet angioedema of the lips (Figure 3). On admission, the blood pressure was 140/80 mm Hg and breath sounds were absent at lung bases. At ultrasound examination, the kidneys appeared normal.

findings.evidence: Caption describes a vessel completely infiltrated by inflammatory cells; in-text states the resected colon showed acute necrotizing vasculitis of submucosal vessels with fibrinoid necrosis

panels.rationale: This is a real patient H&E histology image of resected colon from a patient diagnosed with hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis, showing a submucosal vessel with inflammatory infiltrate and fibrinoid necrosis consistent with necrotizing vasculitis, a recognized manifestation of the disease. The red arrow annotation highlights the affected vessel.
panels.attribution_text: Jost et al. A Case of Hypocomplementemic Urticarial Vasculitis Syndrome With Severe Renal and Gastrointestinal Involvement.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.72113. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 8.
panels.figure_caption: Light microscopy of the colon resectate. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stain. Light microscopy showing a vessel, which has been completely infiltrated by inflammatory cells (red arrow).
in_text_mentions: colonoscopy in the cecum and the ascending colon, though no clear occlusions of large or medium-sized vessels were evident on abdominal CT angiography (Figure 6). Subsequently, the patient became septic with guarding and rebound tenderness, and an emergent laparotomy was performed. Intraoperatively, almost the entire colon was found to be ischemic; thus, subtotal colectomy with terminal ileostomy was necessary. Light microscopy of the resected colon showed acute necrotizing vasculitis of submucosal vessels, i.e., fibrinoid necrosis, alongside fresh intravascular fibrin-thrombi (Figures 7, 8).

plate_findings.evidence: Caption: multiple wheals involving the décolleté region, upper extremities, epigastrium (a); in-text: disseminated dermatosis characterized by multiple wheals of variable sizes, pale pink, smooth surface, well-defined borders, soft consistency lasting more than 24 hours

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Clinical photograph of a patient with hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis showing multiple persistent urticarial wheals in the décolleté, upper extremities, and epigastrium, consistent with the disease's characteristic cutaneous manifestation. b: Clinical photograph of a patient with hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis showing persistent urticarial wheals in the décolleté and upper chest region, consistent with the disease's cutaneous presentation. c: Clinical photograph of a patient with hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis showing persistent urticarial wheals in the paravertebral and supra-scapular regions, consistent with the disease's disseminated cutaneous involvement.
panels.attribution_text: Aparicio et al. Hypocomplementemic Urticarial Vasculitis: A Case Report.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.100143. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Cutaneous manifestations of hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis Patient with an eight-month evolution disseminated dermatosis characterized by multiple wheals involving the décolleté region, upper extremities, epigastrium (a)(b), paravertebral area, and supra-scapular region (c).
in_text_mentions: epartment. At the time of evaluation, both the cutaneous manifestations and arthralgias had been present for eight months. During the physical examination, we observed a disseminated dermatosis on the upper extremities involving the lateral aspects of both arms, the décolleté area, the upper third of the back, and the epigastrium. The dermatosis was characterized by multiple wheals of variable sizes (the largest measuring 6 cm), pale pink, with a smooth surface, well-defined borders, and soft consistency. These lesions caused intense pruritus and typically lasted more than 24 hours (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Low-power H&E histology (10×) showing skin biopsy features of hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis with dermal edema and perivascular mixed inflammatory infiltrate. b: High-power H&E histology (200×) demonstrating leukocytoclastic vasculitis with neutrophils, eosinophils, nuclear dust, and fibrinoid necrosis in a patient with hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis.
panels.attribution_text: Aparicio et al. Hypocomplementemic Urticarial Vasculitis: A Case Report.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.100143. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Histological examination of the affected skin Skin biopsy (H&E stain) demonstrates edema in the superficial dermis with a mixed perivascular infiltrate extending into the reticular dermis (panel a, 10×), with a predominance of neutrophils, eosinophils, and marked nuclear dust (panel b, 200×).
in_text_mentions: The biopsy revealed a perivascular mixed infiltrate with a predominance of neutrophils and eosinophils in the superficial and reticular dermis, along with abundant nuclear dust and mild fibrinoid necrosis (Figure 2). Laboratory studies, performed as part of the diagnostic workup, demonstrated reduced C3 and C4 levels, as well as elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) (Table 1).

in_text_mentions: ion. His blood pressure was 148/80mm Hg, his heart rate was regular at 76 beats/min, and his body temperature was 36.3°C. He had diffuse urticarial lesions on his face, trunk, and upper arms (Figure 1). A skin biopsy of a new urticarial lesion revealed leukocytoclastic vasculitis. An abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan revealed multifocal low-attenuated lesions in both kidneys without other abnormalities. A laboratory workup showed his levels of total protein to be 5.7g/dL, albumin 3.3g/dL, BUN 21mg/dL, creatinine 1.38mg/dL, D-dimer 3.5μg/mL (normal range, 0 to 1μg/mL), fibrinogen 481mg/dL

panels.figure_caption: Perivascular inflammatory infiltrate comprising predominantly neutrophils with red cell extravasation and perivascular edema suggestive of leukocytoclastic vasculitis using hematoxylin and eosin stain (H&E) (A) and high-power view (100x magnification) showing numerous neutrophils and lymphocytes in the dermis (B). Methyl violet stain was positive in mast cells, which confirms urticarial vasculitis.
